DIF analysis via Andersen's likelihood-ratio test

Source: R/dif_lr.R
RMdifLR.Rd

Fits a Rasch model by conditional maximum likelihood in the full sample and in each group of an external grouping variable, tests the difference with Andersen's likelihood-ratio test, and reports per-group item locations (or per-group threshold locations) together with their standard errors. level (item or threshold) and output (data.frame, kable or ggplot) give six views of the same fits.

Usage

RMdifLR(
  data,
  dif_var,
  model = c("auto", "PCM", "RM"),
  level = c("item", "threshold"),
  output = c("kable", "dataframe", "ggplot"),
  cutoff = 0.5,
  conf = 0.95,
  sort = FALSE
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or matrix of item responses (non-negative integers, 0-based). One column per item, one row per person. Person IDs and grouping variables must not be included – pass the grouping variable separately via dif_var.

dif_var

Vector of length nrow(data) (factor, character, or numeric) defining the DIF grouping variable. Coerced to factor; unused levels are dropped. Rows where dif_var is NA are dropped with a message. Must result in at least 2 groups after cleaning.

model

One of "auto" (default), "PCM", or "RM". "auto" fits the Rasch model when the data are dichotomous (max response = 1) and the partial credit model otherwise (the two coincide for dichotomous data). "RM" errors on polytomous data.

level

One of "item" (default) or "threshold". "item" reports each item's mean threshold location per group; "threshold" reports each individual threshold per group. For dichotomous (RM) data the two views are equivalent (one threshold per item).

output

One of "kable" (default), "dataframe", or "ggplot". The data.frame has a logical Flagged column (unless cutoff = NULL), the kable bolds flagged rows, and the ggplot shows confidence intervals.

cutoff

Numeric or NULL. Threshold (in logits) for the Flagged column: a row is flagged when MaxDiff > cutoff, where MaxDiff is the difference between the largest and smallest per-group location for that item (or threshold). Set to NULL to suppress flagging. Default 0.5. This default is a convention in applied Rasch work (Jin et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Pickard et al., 2006), not a value with a statistical or substantive justification. See Details.

conf

Numeric in (0, 1). Confidence level used for the ggplot error bars. Default 0.95.

sort

Logical. Sort the rows of the data.frame and kable output by MaxDiff (descending). Default FALSE.

Value

A data.frame, a knitr_kable object, or a ggplot object, depending on output.

The data.frame has one row per item (level = "item") or per item x threshold (level = "threshold"), with columns Item (and Threshold at threshold level), one numeric column per group level, an All column for the unsplit fit, MaxDiff, Flagged (when cutoff is non-NULL), and matching SE_* columns.

The Andersen LR test result is attached as attr(result, "lr_test") on the data.frame, in the kable footnote, and in the ggplot caption (LR \(\chi^2\), df, p-value).

Details

The Partial Credit Model (PCM) is fitted by default for polytomous data and the dichotomous Rasch Model (RM) is fitted when all responses are 0/1; this can be overridden via model.

Each fit is a CML partial credit model from psychotools::pcmodel() (a dichotomous item is a 2-category PCM). Within each fit the thresholds sum to zero, as in RMitemParameters, so each group's locations are centred on that group's own mean threshold. The All column is the fit to the full dataset. An item's location is the mean of its thresholds, and its SE is the SE of that mean, computed from the thresholds' covariance matrix.

The Andersen LR statistic is twice the difference between the sum of the group conditional log-likelihoods and the full-sample one, with df equal to the extra free parameters of the group fits. It equals eRm::LRtest() on the same data. Respondents with missing responses are kept (CML uses the items they answered).

Response categories. Every category an item uses must be used in every group, or that item's thresholds cannot be compared across groups. The same holds when a category is used in a group only by respondents with a zero or perfect score there, since CML leaves them out and the threshold cannot be estimated. The function then stops and names the items, categories and groups (eRm::LRtest() instead left items with an unused category out of the test without saying so, and returned diverging estimates in the second case). With small groups this is common for sparse categories: merge them with an adjacent one, combine groups, or leave the item out.

DIF size and the cutoff. The Flagged column applies one fixed cutoff to MaxDiff, and no single value suits every scale. An appropriate cutoff depends on the number of items, the number of response categories and the type of DIF (Van de Winckel et al., 2022). Treat a flag as a prompt for a closer look, not as a verdict. Judging DIF means weighing its size against its practical consequences (Henninger et al., 2025). These are best evaluated by simulation: estimate person locations with and without accounting for DIF, for instance by splitting the affected item by group, and check whether the difference changes substantive conclusions (Johansson et al., 2026). For polytomous items, DIF can differ between an item's thresholds, which level = "threshold" shows (Henninger et al., 2025). MaxDiff is a point estimate, and with small groups its uncertainty is large (see the SE_* columns). The LR test addresses a different question: whether any DIF is present, not how large it is.

Real and artificial DIF. Real DIF in one item induces artificial DIF in the other items, in the opposite direction (Hagquist & Andrich, 2017). Here the mechanism is direct: each group's locations are centred on that group's own mean threshold, so a real shift in one item moves the other items' locations the other way. An item can therefore be flagged only because another item has DIF, and one analysis cannot tell real from artificial DIF. Hagquist and Andrich (2017) recommend resolving DIF items one at a time, starting with the item with the largest DIF (for instance by splitting it into group-specific items), and repeating the analysis before deciding on the next. Do not overinterpret the flags from a single run.

References

Andersen, E. B. (1973). A goodness of fit test for the Rasch model. Psychometrika, 38(1), 123-140. doi:10.1007/BF02291180

Hagquist, C., & Andrich, D. (2017). Recent advances in analysis of differential item functioning in health research using the Rasch model. Health and Quality of Life Outcomes, 15, 181. doi:10.1186/s12955-017-0755-0

Henninger, M., Radek, J., Sengewald, M.-A., & Strobl, C. (2025). Partial credit trees meet the partial gamma coefficient for quantifying DIF and DSF in polytomous items. Behaviormetrika, 52(2), 221-257. doi:10.1007/s41237-024-00252-3

Jin, Y., Myers, N. D., Ahn, S., & Penfield, R. D. (2013). A comparison of uniform DIF effect size estimators under the MIMIC and Rasch models. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 73(2), 339-358. doi:10.1177/0013164412462705

Johansson, M., Preuter, M., & Melin, J. (2026). Valid and reliable? Basic criteria and modern methods for assessing psychometric quality. OSF Preprints. doi:10.31219/osf.io/3htzc_v2

Kim, S., Ouellet, L. J., Mazza, J., & Spaulding, A. C. (2017). Rasch analysis and differential item functioning of a social support measure in jail inmates with HIV infection. Evaluation & the Health Professions, 40(1), 33-60. doi:10.1177/0163278716644954

Pickard, A. S., Dalal, M. R., & Bushnell, D. M. (2006). A comparison of depressive symptoms in stroke and primary care: Applying Rasch models to evaluate the Center for Epidemiologic Studies-Depression Scale. Value in Health, 9(1), 59-64. doi:10.1111/j.1524-4733.2006.00082.x

Strobl, C., Kopf, J., & Zeileis, A. (2015). Rasch trees: A new method for detecting differential item functioning in the Rasch model. Psychometrika, 80(2), 289-316. doi:10.1007/s11336-013-9388-3

Van de Winckel, A., Kozlowski, A. J., Johnston, M. V., Weaver, J., Grampurohit, N., Terhorst, L., Juengst, S., Ehrlich-Jones, L., Heinemann, A. W., Melvin, J., Sood, P., & Mallinson, T. (2022). Reporting guideline for RULER: Rasch reporting guideline for rehabilitation research: Explanation and elaboration. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, 103(7), 1487-1498. doi:10.1016/j.apmr.2022.03.019

See also

RMdifGamma, with simulation-based cutoffs from RMdifGammaCutoff, and RMdifTree, for continuous DIF variables and interactions between them (Strobl et al., 2015; Henninger et al., 2025).

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("eRm", quietly = TRUE)) { # for the example data
  set.seed(1)
  data("pcmdat2", package = "eRm")
  grp <- factor(sample(c("A", "B"), nrow(pcmdat2), replace = TRUE))

  # Default: kable of per-group item locations
  RMdifLR(pcmdat2, dif_var = grp)

  # ggplot panel of item locations with 95% CIs
  RMdifLR(pcmdat2, dif_var = grp, output = "ggplot")

  # Threshold-level kable, sorted by MaxDiff
  RMdifLR(pcmdat2, dif_var = grp, level = "threshold", sort = TRUE)

  # Tidy data.frame for downstream use
  df <- RMdifLR(pcmdat2, dif_var = grp, output = "dataframe")
  attr(df, "lr_test")
  df[df$Flagged, ]
}
#> [1] Item    A       B       All     MaxDiff Flagged SE_A    SE_B    SE_All 
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
# }
